claims.text: Protective-scale development in high-entropy alloys is driven by controlled diffusion of reactive elements such as Si, Cr, or Al from a chemically complex alloy matrix.
Reactive-element diffusion produces an in situ dual-layer scale consisting of an inner silicide or intermetallic layer and an outer oxide layer.
The inner silicide or intermetallic layer mechanically anchors the protective scale to the substrate.
The outer oxide layer grows slowly and acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress.
The inner and outer layers together confer superior oxidation resistance.
The relevant initial alloy contains multiple reactive elements such as Si, Cr, or Al within a fine, heterogeneous microstructure.
Preexisting silicide or intermetallic particles may be present in the initial alloy.
Exposure to a high-temperature oxygen-containing environment causes formation of the proposed outer-oxide/inner-silicide structure.
Chemical complexity causes selective, kinetically limited diffusion of particular reactive elements.
The dual-layer scale self-heals through replenishment of protective phases.
An optimized alloy will develop a stable, continuous dual-layer structure.
An optimized alloy will exhibit lower oxidation mass gain than a control lacking optimized reactive-element partitioning.
Alloys without sufficient reactive-element diffusion control form discontinuous or rapidly growing oxide scales and consequently oxidize faster.
The proposed mechanism applies from 700 °C to 900 °C.
The proposed mechanism applies in atmospheres where oxygen diffusion is the dominant oxidative process.
Changes in alloy composition or exposure beyond the stated temperature range may alter reactive-element diffusion and scale stability.
